questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The volume occupied at STP by 3.2 g of sulphur dioxide gas is (S = 32, O = 16; molar volume of a gas at STP = 22.7 L mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Converting a mass of gas into its volume at STP
solution.explanation: Find the amount of SO₂ in moles from its molar mass and multiply by the molar volume.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.27 L uses 32 g mol⁻¹ (the mass of S only) as the molar mass. 0.568 L uses 128 g mol⁻¹, twice the correct molar mass. 3.405 L multiplies by 3, counting atoms instead of molecules.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', mole concept and molar masses

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a postulate of Dalton's atomic theory?

options.text: All the atoms of a given element have identical properties, including identical mass.
Compounds are formed when atoms of different elements combine in a fixed ratio.
Atoms are made up of protons, neutrons and electrons.

solution.concept: Postulates of Dalton's atomic theory
solution.explanation: Dalton (1808) took atoms to be indivisible. The sub-atomic particles were discovered much later, so a statement about protons, neutrons and electrons cannot be one of his postulates.
steps: Indivisible atoms, identical atoms of an element, fixed-ratio combination → Dalton's postulates
Atoms made of sub-atomic particles → contradicts the idea of indivisible atoms
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three statements are postulates of Dalton's theory as given in NCERT.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', Dalton's atomic theory
solution.final_answer: Option D: Atoms are made up of protons, neutrons and electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: 14 g of nitrogen gas (N₂) contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms of nitrogen (N = 14).
Statement II: One mole of solid sodium chloride contains 6.022 × 10²³ ions in all.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Counting atoms and ions with the mole concept
solution.explanation: 14 g of N₂ is 14/28 = 0.5 mol of molecules; each molecule has two atoms, so it contains 1 mol (6.022 × 10²³) of N atoms. Statement I is true. One mole of NaCl contains one mole of Na⁺ and one mole of Cl⁻, i.e. 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ ions in all. Statement II is false.
steps: I: n(N₂) = 0.5 mol → n(N) = 1 mol → 6.022 × 10²³ atoms → true
II: 1 mol NaCl → 1 mol Na⁺ + 1 mol Cl⁻ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ ions → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II counts formula units, not ions; Statement I correctly uses two atoms per N₂ molecule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', mole concept and molar masses
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 0.30 g of an organic compound containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen gives 0.44 g of CO₂ and 0.18 g of H₂O on complete combustion. The vapour density of the compound is 30. Its molecular formula is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16; molar mass = 2 × vapour density):

solution.concept: Empirical formula from combustion data; molecular formula from vapour density
solution.explanation: Find the masses of C and H from the CO₂ and H₂O formed, get O by difference, convert to a mole ratio, then compare the empirical formula mass with the molar mass (2 × vapour density).
steps: Moles: C 0.01, H 0.02, O 0.01 → empirical formula CH₂O (formula mass 30)
solution.why_others_wrong: CH₂O is only the empirical formula (it takes the molar mass equal to the vapour density). C₄H₈O₄ uses a molar mass of 120 g mol⁻¹. C₂H₂O₂ counts one H atom per H₂O molecule instead of two.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', empirical and molecular formula

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The mass of calcium carbonate that contains the same number of oxygen atoms as 8.8 g of carbon dioxide is (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16):

solution.concept: Equating numbers of atoms through the mole concept
solution.explanation: Find the moles of O atoms in the CO₂ (two per molecule); CaCO₃ has three O atoms per formula unit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20.0 g equates moles of CaCO₃ with moles of CO₂. 40.0 g takes one O atom per CaCO₃. 6.67 g takes one O atom per CO₂ molecule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', mole concept and molar masses

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At the same temperature and pressure, two volumes of hydrogen react with one volume of oxygen to give two volumes of water vapour, in agreement with the equation 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g).
Reason (R): Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Gay-Lussac's law explained by Avogadro's law
solution.explanation: By Avogadro's law, volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure are proportional to the numbers of molecules. A 2 : 1 : 2 volume ratio is therefore a 2 : 1 : 2 ratio of molecules, which is exactly what the balanced equation (with diatomic H₂ and O₂) requires. R explains A.
steps: Volume ratio = molecule ratio (because of R) → matches the equation → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and Avogadro's hypothesis is precisely what converts the volume ratio into the mole ratio of the equation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes and Avogadro's law
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Haemoglobin contains 0.34% iron by mass, and each haemoglobin molecule contains four iron atoms. The molar mass of haemoglobin is about (Fe = 56):

solution.concept: Molar mass from the mass per cent of a minor element
solution.explanation: In one mole of haemoglobin there are 4 mol of Fe, i.e. 224 g of iron, and this is 0.34% of the molar mass.
steps: Mass of Fe per mole of haemoglobin = 4 × 56 = 224 g
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.65 × 10⁴ g mol⁻¹ assumes one Fe atom per molecule. 6.59 × 10² g mol⁻¹ divides by 0.34 instead of 0.0034. 2.64 × 10⁵ g mol⁻¹ multiplies the correct value by 4 again.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', percentage composition

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At the same temperature and pressure, one volume of the vapour of an element X combines exactly with six volumes of hydrogen gas (H₂) to give four volumes of a gaseous hydride. Each molecule of the hydride contains one atom of X and three atoms of hydrogen. The number of atoms in one molecule of the vapour of X is:

solution.concept: Gay-Lussac's law with Avogadro's law: atomicity from combining volumes
solution.explanation: Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules, so 1 molecule of Xₙ reacts with 6 molecules of H₂ to give 4 molecules of XH₃. All the X atoms of one Xₙ molecule end up in four hydride molecules.
steps: X atoms: n = 4 × 1 = 4 → the vapour is X₄
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 ignores Avogadro's law. 2 assumes the vapour is diatomic like most gases; then only two volumes of hydride would form. 6 is the number of volumes of hydrogen, not the atomicity of X.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry', Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes and Avogadro's law

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The ratio of the energy of a photon of wavelength 400 nm to that of a photon of wavelength 600 nm is:

solution.concept: Energy of a photon, E = hc/λ
solution.explanation: Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so the shorter-wavelength photon carries more energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 3 takes E proportional to λ. 9 : 4 and 4 : 9 square the ratio, as if E depended on 1/λ² or λ².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Planck's quantum theory

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantum numbers of an electron) with List-II (subshell in which the electron is present).

List-I:
A. n = 3, l = 2
B. n = 4, l = 3
C. n = 2, l = 1
D. n = 5, l = 0

List-II:
I. 5s
II. 3d
III. 2p
IV. 4f

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Naming subshells from n and l
solution.explanation: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d, f; the subshell is written as n followed by this letter.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each other code gives at least one wrong letter for l, e.g. pairing l = 3 with p or l = 1 with f.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', quantum numbers
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In vacuum, radio waves travel faster than X-rays.
Statement II: The frequency (ν) and wavelength (λ) of an electromagnetic radiation are related by c = νλ, where c is the speed of light.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Characteristics of electromagnetic radiation
solution.explanation: All electromagnetic radiations, whatever their wavelength, travel with the same speed in vacuum, 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, so Statement I is false. c = νλ is the relation between frequency and wavelength, so Statement II is true.
steps: I: all EM radiations have the same speed in vacuum → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Radio waves and X-rays differ in frequency and wavelength, not in their speed in vacuum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', nature of electromagnetic radiation
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: According to Bohr's model, the radius of the nth orbit of a hydrogen-like species is rₙ = 52.9 (n²/Z) pm. The orbit of the Be³⁺ ion (Z = 4) whose radius equals that of the first Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom is:

solution.concept: Radius of Bohr orbits of hydrogen-like species
solution.explanation: Set 52.9 n²/4 equal to 52.9 pm (n = 1, Z = 1 for hydrogen) and solve for n.
solution.why_others_wrong: n = 4 takes r proportional to n/Z. n = 16 confuses n² with Z². n = 1 gives a radius of 13.2 pm, a quarter of the hydrogen value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Bohr's model for hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following electronic configurations represents an EXCITED state, not the ground state, of the atom named?

solution.concept: Ground-state configurations by the Aufbau principle, with the Cr and Cu exceptions
solution.explanation: The ground state of carbon is 1s² 2s² 2p²; promoting one 2s electron to 2p gives an excited state. The chromium and copper configurations, though exceptions to the simple filling order, are their actual ground states (half-filled and filled 3d subshells are extra stable).
solution.why_others_wrong: Students often mark Cr or Cu because they do not follow the simple Aufbau order, but these are the observed ground-state configurations.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', electronic configuration of atoms; stability of half-filled and completely filled orbitals

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): There is no 3f subshell.
Reason (R): For n = 3, the azimuthal quantum number l can have only the values 0, 1 and 2, whereas an f subshell needs l = 3.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Allowed values of the azimuthal quantum number
solution.explanation: l can take the values 0 to (n − 1). For n = 3 this means 0, 1, 2 (3s, 3p, 3d); l = 3 (f) first becomes possible at n = 4. R is exactly the reason A is true.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, and the restriction on l in R is what rules out a 3f subshell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', quantum numbers
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An electron and a proton have the same uncertainty in velocity. The ratio of the minimum uncertainty in the position of the electron to that of the proton is (mass of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; mass of proton = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg):

solution.concept: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, Δx × mΔv ≥ h/4π
solution.explanation: For the same Δv, the minimum Δx = h/(4πmΔv) is inversely proportional to the mass, so the much lighter electron has the far larger uncertainty in position.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 1833 inverts the ratio (takes Δx proportional to mass). 1 : 1 ignores the mass in Δp = mΔv. 42.8 : 1 takes a square root that is not in the relation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the emission spectrum of atomic hydrogen are correct?

(a) The lines of the Lyman series lie in the ultraviolet region.
(b) The lines of the Paschen series lie in the infrared region.
(c) Within a series, the lines come closer together as the wavelength decreases towards the series limit.
(d) The longest-wavelength line of the Lyman series arises from the transition n = 3 → n = 1.
(e) The Balmer series arises when electrons fall to the orbit n = 1.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Spectral series of hydrogen
solution.explanation: Lyman (n₁ = 1) lies in the ultraviolet, Balmer (n₁ = 2) in the visible and Paschen (n₁ = 3) in the infrared. Since 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), successive lines of a series crowd together towards the series limit (n₂ → ∞), which is the short-wavelength end. The longest wavelength of a series is the smallest energy gap, n₂ = n₁ + 1.
steps: (c) lines converge at the short-wavelength limit ✓
(e) Balmer ends at n = 2, not n = 1 ✗
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (d) or (e) is wrong; (a) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', line spectrum of hydrogen

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Combine Bohr's condition mvr = nh/2π with the de Broglie relation λ = h/mv to find the de Broglie wavelength of the electron in the third orbit (n = 3) of a hydrogen atom. (Radius of the nth orbit = 52.9 n² pm; π = 3.14)

solution.concept: Electron waves in Bohr orbits: nλ = 2πr
solution.explanation: From mvr = nh/2π, mv = nh/2πr, so λ = h/mv = 2πr/n: a whole number of wavelengths fits round the orbit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 332 pm is the wavelength in the first orbit (2πr₁). 2990 pm forgets to divide by n. 498 pm uses πr/n instead of 2πr/n.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', Bohr's model; dual behaviour of matter

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about filling electrons into orbitals are correct?

(a) The 4s orbital is filled before the 3d orbitals because its (n + l) value is lower.
(b) In the Aufbau order, the 4f orbitals are filled after the 6s orbital and before the 5d orbitals.
(c) Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity applies to the filling of orbitals of equal energy.
(d) A single orbital can hold two electrons with the same spin.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Aufbau principle, (n + l) rule, Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle
solution.explanation: 4s has n + l = 4 and 3d has n + l = 5, so 4s fills first. The filling order runs …, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, …. Hund's rule concerns degenerate orbitals such as the three p or five d orbitals. By the Pauli principle, two electrons in one orbital must have opposite spins.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options including (d) break the exclusion principle; '(a) and (c) only' wrongly rejects the correct filling order in (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', filling of orbitals in atoms

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Particle A has twice the mass of particle B, but its kinetic energy is one-eighth of that of B. The ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths, λ_A : λ_B, is:

solution.concept: de Broglie wavelength in terms of kinetic energy
solution.explanation: Momentum p = √(2mK), so λ = h/p = h/√(2mK); the wavelength is inversely proportional to √(mK).
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 inverts the ratio. 4 : 1 and 1 : 4 leave out the square root (taking λ ∝ 1/(mK)).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Structure of Atom', dual behaviour of matter

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the Kössel–Lewis description of ionic bonding, the electrovalence of an element equals the number of unit charges on its ion. In calcium fluoride, CaF₂, the electrovalences of calcium and fluorine are respectively:

solution.concept: Electrovalence in ionic compounds
solution.explanation: Calcium (2 valence electrons) loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺; each fluorine atom (7 valence electrons) gains one electron to form F⁻. CaF₂ = Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻.
solution.why_others_wrong: '1 and 2' swaps the two values, reading the subscript 2 in CaF₂ as the charge on fluoride. '2 and 2' and '1 and 1' do not match the ions Ca²⁺ and F⁻.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', Kössel–Lewis approach; ionic or electrovalent bond

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (molecule) with List-II (its bond angle).

List-I:
A. BeCl₂
B. BF₃
C. CH₄
D. H₂O

List-II:
I. 104.5°
II. 120°
III. 180°
IV. 109.5°

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Bond angles predicted by VSEPR theory
solution.explanation: BeCl₂ is linear (two bond pairs), BF₃ trigonal planar (three bond pairs), CH₄ tetrahedral (four bond pairs). In H₂O two lone pairs squeeze the H–O–H angle from 109.5° down to 104.5°.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes either swap the planar and tetrahedral angles or give water the ideal tetrahedral angle, ignoring lone pair repulsion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In H₂, O₂ and Cl₂ the shared electron pair is shared equally between the two identical atoms, so the bond is a non-polar covalent bond.
Statement II: In the HF molecule, the shared electron pair is displaced towards the hydrogen atom.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Polar and non-polar covalent bonds
solution.explanation: Between identical atoms the electronegativities are equal, so the pair is shared equally: Statement I is true. Fluorine is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so the pair shifts towards F (H^δ+–F^δ−): Statement II is false.
steps: I: identical atoms → equal sharing → non-polar → true
II: pair shifts towards the more electronegative F, not H → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the direction of polarity; F carries the partial negative charge in HF.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', polarity of bonds
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In which of the following molecules does the central atom have fewer than eight electrons in its valence shell (an incomplete octet)?

solution.concept: Limitations of the octet rule: the incomplete octet
solution.explanation: Beryllium has only two valence electrons; in BeH₂ it forms two bonds and is surrounded by just four electrons. Carbon in CO₂ and CH₄, and nitrogen in NH₃ (three bond pairs + one lone pair), have complete octets.
steps: BeH₂: 2 bond pairs → 4 electrons around Be
CO₂, CH₄: 4 bonds → octet; NH₃: 3 bp + 1 lp → octet
solution.why_others_wrong: CO₂, NH₃ and CH₄ all obey the octet rule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', limitations of the octet rule

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a Lewis structure of ozone, O=O–O, in which every atom has an octet, the central oxygen atom carries one lone pair. The formal charge on the central oxygen atom is:

solution.concept: Formal charge = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − ½ (bonding electrons)
solution.explanation: The central O is joined by one double and one single bond (six bonding electrons) and holds one lone pair (two non-bonding electrons).
steps: Check: double-bonded terminal O 6 − 4 − 2 = 0; single-bonded terminal O 6 − 6 − 1 = −1; total 0 for the neutral molecule
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 and −1 are the formal charges of the two terminal oxygen atoms. +2 ignores the lone pair on the central atom.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', formal charge

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The numbers of σ bonds and π bonds in one molecule of tetracyanoethylene, (NC)₂C=C(CN)₂, are respectively:

solution.concept: Counting σ and π bonds: every bond has one σ; a double bond adds one π, a triple bond two π
solution.explanation: The molecule has one C=C bond, four C–C single bonds (each joining a CN group to the central carbon) and four C≡N triple bonds.
solution.why_others_wrong: '9 and 5' counts only one π bond per triple bond. '13 and 9' counts π bonds of the triple bonds as σ bonds as well. '5 and 9' leaves out the σ bonds of the C≡N groups.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', types of overlapping and nature of covalent bonds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The PCl₅ molecule is quite reactive.
Reason (R): In trigonal bipyramidal PCl₅, the two axial P–Cl bonds suffer greater repulsion from the equatorial bond pairs, so they are slightly longer and weaker than the three equatorial bonds.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Axial and equatorial bonds in PCl₅
solution.explanation: NCERT explains the reactivity of PCl₅ by its axial bonds: each axial bond pair is at 90° to three equatorial bond pairs, is repelled more, and becomes longer and weaker. These weaker bonds break easily, which makes the molecule reactive. R explains A.
steps: Axial bonds: 3 bond pairs at 90° → more repulsion → longer, weaker
Weak axial bonds → PCl₅ reactive → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the weaker axial bonds are the stated cause of the reactivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', hybridisation: formation of PCl₅
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Taking z as the internuclear axis, which of the following overlaps of atomic orbitals of two atoms lead to a σ bond?

(a) 1s with 1s
(b) 1s with 2p_z
(c) 2p_z with 2p_z
(d) 2pₓ with 2pₓ
(e) 1s with 2pₓ

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Types of orbital overlap: σ (head-on) and π (sideways)
solution.explanation: s–s, s–p_z and p_z–p_z overlaps take place head-on along the internuclear axis and give σ bonds. Two pₓ orbitals overlap sideways and give a π bond. A 1s and a 2pₓ orbital give zero net overlap when z is the bond axis.
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) gives a π bond, not a σ bond, and (e) gives no bond at all.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', types of overlapping and nature of covalent bonds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The covalent character of the silver halides decreases from AgF to AgI, because the iodide ion is the largest of the halide ions.
Statement II: MgCl₂ has greater covalent character than NaCl, because Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and a smaller size than Na⁺.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Fajans' rules: polarising power of cations and polarisability of anions
solution.explanation: A larger anion is more easily polarised, so covalent character INCREASES from AgF to AgI: Statement I is false (its reason is right but its conclusion reversed). A cation of higher charge and smaller size polarises the anion more, so MgCl₂ is more covalent than NaCl: Statement II is true.
steps: I: larger anion → more polarisable → more covalent → order is AgF < AgCl < AgBr < AgI → false
II: Mg²⁺ (2+, smaller) polarises Cl⁻ more than Na⁺ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I draws the wrong conclusion from a correct fact about the size of iodide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', polarity of bonds (partial covalent character of ionic bonds)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The He₂ molecule does not exist.
Reason (R): In He₂ the numbers of electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals are equal, so its bond order is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Bond order and stability in molecular orbital theory
solution.explanation: He₂ has four electrons: σ1s² σ*1s². Bond order = ½(2 − 2) = 0; the antibonding electrons cancel the stabilisation by the bonding electrons, so no stable molecule forms. R explains A.
steps: Bond order = ½(N_b − N_a) = ½(2 − 2) = 0 → not stable
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the zero bond order is the reason given by MO theory.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', molecular orbital theory: bond order
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Using the molecular orbital energy order for species with up to 14 electrons (π2pₓ = π2p_y below σ2p_z), the bond order and the magnetic behaviour of the C₂²⁻ ion are:

solution.concept: Molecular orbital configuration of an ion isoelectronic with N₂
solution.explanation: C₂²⁻ has 6 + 6 + 2 = 14 electrons, the same as N₂: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² (π2pₓ² = π2p_y²) σ2p_z². All the electrons are paired.
solution.why_others_wrong: '2; diamagnetic' is C₂ (12 electrons); the two extra electrons of C₂²⁻ enter the bonding σ2p_z orbital, raising the bond order to 3. Paramagnetic options would need unpaired electrons, of which there are none.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', molecular orbital theory

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (species) with List-II (its shape predicted by VSEPR theory).

List-I:
A. I₃⁻
B. ClO₃⁻
C. SF₅⁻
D. NO₂⁻

List-II:
I. Bent
II. Square pyramidal
III. Linear
IV. Trigonal pyramidal

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Shapes of ions from the numbers of bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom
solution.explanation: Count the electron pairs on the central atom: I₃⁻, central I has 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs (AB₂E₃, linear); ClO₃⁻, Cl has 3 bp + 1 lp (AB₃E, trigonal pyramidal); SF₅⁻, S has 5 bp + 1 lp (AB₅E, square pyramidal); NO₂⁻, N has 2 σ bond pairs + 1 lp (AB₂E, bent).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes ignore lone pairs, e.g. calling ClO₃⁻ planar-like or NO₂⁻ linear.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The dipole moment of the water molecule is 1.85 D and its H–O–H bond angle is 104.5°. Treating the molecular dipole as just the vector sum of the two O–H bond dipoles, the dipole moment of one O–H bond is (cos 52.25° = 0.612):

solution.concept: Resultant of two equal bond dipoles at an angle
solution.explanation: Each bond dipole μ makes an angle of 104.5°/2 = 52.25° with the bisector, so the resultant is 2μ cos 52.25°.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.925 D simply halves the molecular dipole, ignoring the angle. 1.13 D multiplies by cos 52.25° instead of dividing. 3.02 D forgets the factor 2 for the two bonds.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', dipole moment

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following shows the correct order of the carbon–oxygen bond length in carbon monoxide (:C≡O:), carbon dioxide and the carbonate ion?

solution.concept: Bond order and bond length; average bond order in a resonance hybrid
solution.explanation: The higher the bond order between the same two atoms, the shorter the bond. CO has a triple bond (bond order 3); in CO₂ each C–O bond has bond order 2 (115 pm, between C=O and C≡O values according to NCERT's resonance description); in the carbonate ion one double bond is shared over three C–O bonds, bond order 4/3.
steps: Bond length is in the reverse order: CO < CO₂ < CO₃²⁻
solution.why_others_wrong: The other orders do not follow the falling bond order 3 > 2 > 4/3; the carbonate ion, with the lowest bond order, has the longest C–O bonds.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', bond parameters; resonance structures

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In the Born–Haber cycle for the formation of NaCl(s) from Na(s) and Cl₂(g), which of the following statements about the signs of the enthalpy changes are correct?

(a) The sublimation of sodium, Na(s) → Na(g), is endothermic.
(b) The electron gain enthalpy of chlorine, Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g), is negative.
(c) The ionisation enthalpy of sodium, Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻, is negative.
(d) The lattice enthalpy, defined for NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), is positive.
(e) The dissociation of Cl₂(g) into chlorine atoms releases energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Energy changes in the formation of an ionic solid
solution.explanation: Breaking up a solid into atoms, removing an electron from an atom and breaking a bond all need energy. Chlorine releases energy when it gains an electron. Separating the ions of a crystal needs a large amount of energy, so the lattice enthalpy as defined is positive (788 kJ mol⁻¹ for NaCl).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options including (c) or (e) contain a wrong sign; '(a) and (d) only' leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', lattice enthalpy; Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Born–Haber cycle

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following shows the molecules in order of INCREASING dipole moment?

solution.concept: Dipole moment from bond polarity, geometry and lone pairs
solution.explanation: Trigonal planar BF₃ has zero dipole moment. In NF₃ the lone pair moment opposes the resultant of the N–F bond moments (0.23 D), whereas in NH₃ they add (1.47 D). Bent H₂O, with two lone pairs and very polar O–H bonds, has 1.85 D.
solution.why_others_wrong: BF₃ must come first (zero dipole moment); NF₃ is below NH₃ because of the opposing lone pair; and H₂O has a larger dipole moment than NH₃.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', dipole moment
solution.final_answer: Option D: BF₃ < NF₃ < NH₃ < H₂O

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In which of the following pairs do the central atoms have the SAME hybridisation but the molecules have DIFFERENT shapes?

solution.concept: Hybridisation versus shape when lone pairs are present
solution.explanation: Xe in XeF₄ (4 bp + 2 lp) and S in SF₆ (6 bp) are both sp³d² hybridised, but XeF₄ is square planar while SF₆ is octahedral, because two of xenon's hybrid orbitals hold lone pairs.
steps: XeF₄: sp³d², square planar; SF₆: sp³d², octahedral → same hybridisation, different shapes ✓
XeF₂ (sp³d) and BeCl₂ (sp): different hybridisation, both linear
BF₃ (sp²) and NH₃ (sp³): different hybridisation; CO₂ and BeCl₂: both sp and both linear
solution.why_others_wrong: XeF₂/BeCl₂ is a trap: same shape but different hybridisation. BF₃/NH₃ differ in both. CO₂/BeCl₂ agree in both.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', VSEPR theory; hybridisation involving d orbitals

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 1 mol of liquid water freezes to ice at 273 K and 1 bar, giving out heat equal to its enthalpy of fusion, 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹, to the surroundings at 273 K. The entropy change of the surroundings is:

solution.concept: Entropy change of the surroundings, ΔS_surr = q_surr/T = −ΔH_system/T
solution.explanation: On freezing, ΔH of the system is −6.01 kJ mol⁻¹; the surroundings absorb this heat at 273 K, so their entropy rises.
solution.why_others_wrong: −22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is the entropy change of the freezing water itself. +0.022 leaves the heat in kJ while reporting J. +1641 multiplies by T instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', entropy and spontaneity

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At a given temperature, the enthalpy of sublimation of a substance is related to its enthalpies of fusion and of vaporisation at the same temperature by:

solution.concept: Hess's law applied to phase changes
solution.explanation: Solid → vapour can be carried out directly, or as solid → liquid followed by liquid → vapour. Enthalpy is a state function, so both routes give the same enthalpy change.
steps: Solid → liquid: ΔfusH; liquid → vapour: ΔvapH
Sum: solid → vapour, ΔsubH = ΔfusH + ΔvapH
solution.why_others_wrong: Subtracting or averaging the two steps has no basis: by Hess's law the enthalpies of successive steps add up.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', enthalpies for different types of reactions (phase transformations); Hess's law

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A spontaneous process can be reversed only by some external agency.
Statement II: Every spontaneous process takes place rapidly.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Meaning of a spontaneous process
solution.explanation: A spontaneous process has a natural tendency to occur in one direction; turning it back needs outside help, so Statement I is true. Spontaneity says nothing about the rate: a spontaneous reaction such as H₂ + O₂ → H₂O at room temperature can be extremely slow. Statement II is false.
steps: I: spontaneous processes are irreversible without an external agency → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Thermodynamics (ΔG) tells whether a process is feasible, not how fast it goes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', spontaneity
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 5 mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly at 300 K from 2 L to 20 L. The entropy change of the gas is (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: ΔS = q_rev/T for an isothermal reversible change
solution.explanation: For the isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas ΔU = 0, so q_rev = −w = 2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i), and ΔS = q_rev/T = 2.303 nR log(V_f/V_i).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 confuses an isothermal process (ΔT = 0) with no entropy change. 41.6 J K⁻¹ leaves out the factor 2.303 when using log₁₀. 2.87 × 10⁴ J K⁻¹ is q_rev (in J), not q_rev/T.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', entropy; work in isothermal reversible expansion

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For an ideal gas, C_p,m = 29.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The heat needed to raise the temperature of 2 mol of this gas by 10 K at constant volume is (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: C_p − C_v = R for an ideal gas; q_V = n C_v ΔT
solution.explanation: At constant volume the heat absorbed equals ΔU = n C_v,m ΔT, and C_v,m = C_p,m − R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 582 J uses C_p (the constant-pressure heat). 166 J uses R in place of C_v. 208 J is for 1 mol only.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', heat capacity; relationship between C_p and C_V for an ideal gas

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The standard enthalpy of formation of I₂(g) at 298 K is not zero.
Reason (R): At 298 K and 1 bar, the reference (most stable) state of iodine is the solid, I₂(s).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Reference states in standard enthalpies of formation
solution.explanation: ΔfH° is zero only for an element in its reference state. For iodine at 298 K this is I₂(s); I₂(g) is formed from it by sublimation, which absorbs heat, so ΔfH°[I₂(g)] is positive (not zero). R explains A.
steps: Reference state of iodine at 298 K = I₂(s) → ΔfH° = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the choice of I₂(s) as the reference state is exactly why I₂(g) has a non-zero value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', standard enthalpy of formation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) For a spontaneous process, the total entropy change of the system and the surroundings is positive.
(b) For a process at equilibrium, the total entropy change of the system and the surroundings is zero.
(c) The entropy of the system increases in every spontaneous process.
(d) Heating a gas at constant volume increases its entropy.
(e) ΔS = q/T gives the entropy change even when the heat q is absorbed irreversibly.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Entropy and the second law
solution.explanation: It is the TOTAL entropy (system + surroundings) that rises in a spontaneous change and stays constant at equilibrium. The system's own entropy may fall (e.g. water freezing below 273 K). Raising the temperature increases molecular motion and entropy. The relation ΔS = q/T uses the heat for a reversible path, q_rev.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) or (e) are wrong; option (a), (c), (d) also drops the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', entropy and spontaneity

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantity, for a closed system) with List-II (its expression).

List-I:
A. Work done on n mol of an ideal gas in a reversible isothermal expansion from V_i to V_f
B. Work done on a gas expanding against a constant external pressure p_ex
C. Heat absorbed at constant volume
D. Heat absorbed at constant pressure

List-II:
I. ΔH
II. −p_ex (V_f − V_i)
III. ΔU
IV. −2.303 nRT log (V_f/V_i)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Expressions for work and heat in the first law
solution.explanation: With the IUPAC sign convention (work done on the system positive): reversible isothermal work is −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i); irreversible work against a constant pressure is −p_ex ΔV; q_V = ΔU and q_p = ΔH.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the reversible and irreversible work expressions or the constant-volume and constant-pressure heats.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', applications: work, enthalpy
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The standard enthalpies of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹) of H₂(g), CH₄(g), C₂H₆(g) and C(graphite) are −286, −890, −1560 and −393.5 respectively. Which fuel gives out the most heat per gram burnt, and how much? (H = 1, C = 12)

solution.concept: Calorific value per gram from molar enthalpies of combustion
solution.explanation: Divide each enthalpy of combustion by the molar mass of the fuel to get the heat given out per gram.
steps: C: 393.5/12 = 32.8 kJ g⁻¹ → hydrogen is the highest
solution.why_others_wrong: Ethane gives the most heat per MOLE, not per gram. Methane is second per gram. Graphite gives the least per gram of the four.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', enthalpy of combustion

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For a reaction, the equilibrium constant is less than 1 at 298 K but greater than 1 at 600 K. Assuming ΔH° and ΔS° do not change with temperature, the signs of ΔH° and ΔS° are:

solution.concept: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −RT ln K
solution.explanation: K < 1 means ΔG° > 0; K > 1 means ΔG° < 0. ΔG° goes from positive at the lower temperature to negative at the higher one only if the TΔS° term, growing with T, overcomes a positive ΔH°, i.e. ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° > 0.
steps: 298 K: ΔG° > 0; 600 K: ΔG° < 0 → ΔG° decreases as T rises → ΔS° > 0
ΔG° > 0 at low T with ΔS° > 0 → ΔH° > 0
solution.why_others_wrong: ΔH° < 0, ΔS° < 0 favours the reaction at LOW temperature (the reverse trend). ΔH° < 0, ΔS° > 0 gives ΔG° < 0 (K > 1) at every temperature. ΔH° > 0, ΔS° < 0 gives K < 1 at every temperature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', Gibbs energy change and equilibrium
solution.final_answer: Option D: ΔH° positive, ΔS° positive

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a system is taken through a complete cycle back to its initial state, ΔU = 0, but the net work done on the system need not be zero.
Statement II: For any cyclic process, the net heat absorbed by the system is zero.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: State functions and path functions in a cyclic process
solution.explanation: U is a state function, so ΔU = 0 for a cycle. Work and heat depend on the path, so a cycle can involve non-zero net work (as in a heat engine): Statement I is true. Then q = ΔU − w = −w, which is zero only if w happens to be zero: Statement II is false.
steps: q + w = 0 → q = −w; w ≠ 0 in general → q ≠ 0 in general
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II treats heat as if it were a state function.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics; state functions
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following can act as a semipermeable membrane in an osmosis experiment, letting solvent molecules pass but not the larger solute molecules?

solution.concept: Semipermeable membranes
solution.explanation: NCERT names membranes of animal or vegetable origin (pig's bladder, parchment) and synthetic ones such as cellophane as semipermeable membranes: they contain a network of submicroscopic holes through which small solvent molecules can pass, but bigger solute molecules cannot.
steps: Filter paper and muslin let solutes through; glass lets nothing through
solution.why_others_wrong: Filter paper and muslin cloth have pores far too large to hold back dissolved solute molecules; glass is impermeable even to the solvent.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', osmosis and osmotic pressure

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At the same temperature, a 1.0 M aqueous solution of glucose has a higher osmotic pressure than a 0.5 M aqueous solution of glucose.
Reason (R): For a dilute solution, the osmotic pressure is proportional to the molar concentration of the solute (π = CRT).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Osmotic pressure and concentration
solution.explanation: π = CRT: at a fixed temperature the osmotic pressure is directly proportional to C, so doubling the molarity doubles π. R explains A.
steps: C doubles from 0.5 M to 1.0 M → π doubles → A follows from R
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the relation in R is the direct reason for A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', osmosis and osmotic pressure
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The relative lowering of vapour pressure of a dilute solution of a non-volatile solute depends on the chemical nature of the solute.
Statement II: At a given temperature, the vapour pressure of a solution of a non-volatile solute in a solvent is lower than that of the pure solvent.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Relative lowering of vapour pressure as a colligative property
solution.explanation: By Raoult's law, (p° − p)/p° = x(solute): it depends only on the proportion of solute particles, not on their nature, so Statement I is false. Solute particles occupy part of the surface and reduce the escaping tendency of the solvent, so the vapour pressure is lowered: Statement II is true.
steps: I: (p° − p)/p° = x₂ → independent of the nature of the solute → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I contradicts the colligative nature of vapour-pressure lowering.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', relative lowering of vapour pressure
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many grams of urea (molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹, non-volatile) must be dissolved in 90 g of water to lower the vapour pressure of the water by 1.0% at a given temperature? Use Raoult's law exactly, (p° − p)/p° = n₂/(n₁ + n₂). (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)

solution.concept: Raoult's law for a solution of a non-volatile solute
solution.explanation: Lowering by 1.0% means the mole fraction of urea is 0.010. Solve n₂/(n₁ + n₂) = 0.010 with n₁ = 5 mol.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.09 g uses the molar mass of glucose (180). 33.3 g reads 1% as a mole fraction of 0.10. 0.303 g reads it as 0.001.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', relative lowering of vapour pressure

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Two aqueous solutions at the same temperature are separated by a semipermeable membrane: compartment X contains 0.10 M urea and compartment Y contains 0.040 M Na₂SO₄ (completely dissociated). What happens?

options.text: Water flows from Y to X, because the urea solution has the higher molarity.
There is no net flow of water, because the two solutions are isotonic.
Urea passes from X to Y until the two molarities become equal.
Water flows from X to Y, because Y has the higher concentration of solute particles.

solution.concept: Osmosis with an electrolyte: the van't Hoff factor
solution.explanation: Osmotic pressure depends on the total concentration of solute particles, iC. Na₂SO₄ → 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻ (i = 3), so Y has 3 × 0.040 = 0.12 M of particles against 0.10 M in X. Solvent moves into the solution with the higher osmotic pressure.
steps: Water moves from X (lower π) to Y (higher π)
solution.why_others_wrong: Comparing molarities without the van't Hoff factor gives the wrong direction. The solutions are not isotonic (0.10 ≠ 0.12). A semipermeable membrane does not let the solute through.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', osmosis; abnormal molar masses (van't Hoff factor)
solution.final_answer: Option D: Water flows from X to Y, because Y has the higher concentration of solute particles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The molal depression constant (K_f) of a solvent depends on the molality of the solution.
Statement II: The molal depression constant of water is 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Cryoscopic constant
solution.explanation: K_f is a property of the solvent alone (ΔT_f = K_f m); the depression ΔT_f depends on molality, but K_f does not. Statement I is false. NCERT lists K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹ for water: Statement II is true.
steps: I: K_f = ΔT_f/m is constant for a given solvent → false
II: K_f(water) = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I confuses ΔT_f, which depends on m, with the constant K_f.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', depression of freezing point
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about osmosis and reverse osmosis are correct?

(a) Reverse osmosis is used for the desalination of sea water.
(b) In reverse osmosis, pure solvent passes from the solution side through the membrane.
(c) A film of cellulose acetate, permeable to water but not to the impurities and ions in sea water, is used as the membrane in desalination by reverse osmosis.
(d) At a given molar concentration and temperature, the osmotic pressure depends on the chemical nature of the non-electrolyte solute.
(e) At a given temperature, the osmotic pressure of a dilute solution is proportional to its molarity.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Osmotic pressure and reverse osmosis
solution.explanation: If a pressure larger than the osmotic pressure is applied to the solution, pure solvent is squeezed out through the membrane: reverse osmosis, used with cellulose acetate membranes to desalinate sea water. π = CRT is a colligative property and does not depend on what the (non-electrolyte) solute is.
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes the false statement (d) or leaves out one of the true ones.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', reverse osmosis and water purification

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A 0.050 m aqueous solution of barium nitrate, Ba(NO₃)₂, freezes at −0.2325 °C. The apparent degree of dissociation of the salt in this solution is (K_f of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; freezing point of water = 0 °C):

solution.concept: Degree of dissociation from the van't Hoff factor
solution.explanation: ΔT_f = iK_f m gives i. For Ba(NO₃)₂ ⇌ Ba²⁺ + 2NO₃⁻ one formula unit gives 3 ions, so i = 1 − α + 3α = 1 + 2α.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50% divides (i − 1) by 3 instead of by (3 − 1). 25% is 1 − α. 60% uses (i − 1)/i.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', abnormal molar masses (van't Hoff factor)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The vapour pressure of a dilute aqueous solution of a non-volatile non-electrolyte is 2.0% lower than that of pure water at the same temperature. Using Raoult's law exactly, the depression in the freezing point of this solution is (K_f of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹):

solution.concept: Linking two colligative properties through the molality
solution.explanation: The 2.0% lowering gives x₂ = 0.020, i.e. n₂/n₁ = 0.020/0.980. Convert this ratio into molality (moles of solute per kg of water), then use ΔT_f = K_f m.
steps: n₂/n₁ = 0.02/0.98 = 0.0204 mol of solute per mol of water
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.037 K multiplies K_f by the mole fraction instead of the molality. 1.13 K is the molality itself (K_f left out). 4.22 K counts a van't Hoff factor of 2 for a non-electrolyte.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', relative lowering of vapour pressure; depression of freezing point

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a dilute solution of a non-volatile solute, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is approximately equal to n₂/n₁, the ratio of the moles of solute to the moles of solvent.
Statement II: At the same temperature, a 1 m aqueous solution of glucose and a 1 m aqueous solution of urea show the same relative lowering of vapour pressure.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Relative lowering of vapour pressure and molality
solution.explanation: x₂ = n₂/(n₁ + n₂) ≈ n₂/n₁ when n₂ ≪ n₁, so Statement I is true. Two 1 m aqueous solutions both contain 1 mol of solute per 1000 g (55.5 mol) of water, so their mole fractions of solute, and hence their relative lowerings, are the same whatever the non-electrolyte: Statement II is true.
steps: I: n₂ ≪ n₁ → x₂ ≈ n₂/n₁ → true
II: same molality, same solvent → same x₂ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: The molar masses of glucose and urea are different, but the relative lowering depends only on the number of moles of solute per mole of solvent, which is equal in equimolal solutions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Solutions', relative lowering of vapour pressure
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The pH of an aqueous solution at 298 K is 4.7. The concentration of H₃O⁺ ions in it is (log 2 = 0.30):

solution.concept: pH = −log[H₃O⁺]; finding the concentration from the pH
solution.explanation: [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ = 10⁻⁴·⁷ = 10⁰·³ × 10⁻⁵, and 10⁰·³ = 2 because log 2 = 0.30.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ is 10⁻⁴·³, which reverses the decimal part of the pH. 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ misplaces the power of ten. 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ is [OH⁻], not [H₃O⁺].
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', the pH scale

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At 298 K, 0.030 g of a gas dissolves in 1.0 L of water when its partial pressure above the water is 1.0 bar. Assuming Henry's law holds, the mass of the gas that dissolves in 1.0 L of water at 298 K when its partial pressure is 3.0 bar is:

solution.concept: Henry's law: solubility of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure
solution.explanation: At constant temperature the mass of gas dissolved in a given amount of solvent is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solvent.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.010 g takes solubility inversely proportional to pressure. 0.030 g ignores the pressure change. 0.27 g takes solubility proportional to p².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', equilibrium involving dissolution of gas in liquids (Henry's law)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For the heterogeneous equilibrium Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g) ⇌ 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g), the expression for K_p is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium constant of a heterogeneous equilibrium
solution.explanation: Pure solids have constant 'concentrations' and are left out of the equilibrium constant expression. Each gaseous partial pressure is raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, products over reactants.
solution.why_others_wrong: The inverted expression is K_p of the reverse reaction. Including solids is incorrect. Dropping the power 4 ignores the coefficients.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', heterogeneous equilibria

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Adding sodium acetate to an aqueous solution of acetic acid decreases the degree of ionisation of the acetic acid.
Reason (R): The acetate ions supplied by the salt shift the equilibrium CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ to the left.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Common ion effect
solution.explanation: Sodium acetate is a strong electrolyte and supplies a large amount of the common ion CH₃COO⁻. By Le Chatelier's principle the ionisation equilibrium of the weak acid shifts to the left, so a smaller fraction of the acid ionises. R explains A.
steps: Equilibrium shifts left → α of CH₃COOH falls
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are true, and the shift caused by the common ion is exactly why the degree of ionisation falls.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', common ion effect in the ionisation of acids and bases
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For the isomerisation A(g) ⇌ B(g), K_c = 4.0 at a certain temperature. 1.0 mol of A is placed in a closed 1.0 L vessel at this temperature. The concentration of B at equilibrium is:

solution.concept: Equilibrium concentrations from K_c
solution.explanation: If x mol L⁻¹ of A changes into B, then [B] = x and [A] = 1.0 − x at equilibrium.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.20 mol L⁻¹ is [A] at equilibrium. 0.25 mol L⁻¹ is 1/K_c. 0.50 mol L⁻¹ assumes K_c = 1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', calculating equilibrium concentrations

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At 298 K, K_a of methanoic acid (HCOOH) is 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ and K_a of ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Using [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(K_a c), the ratio of [H₃O⁺] in a 0.1 M solution of methanoic acid to that in a 0.1 M solution of ethanoic acid is (√10 = 3.16):

solution.concept: Relative strengths of weak acids at the same concentration
solution.explanation: For a weak acid that ionises only slightly, [H₃O⁺] = √(K_a c). At equal c the ratio is √(K_a1/K_a2).
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 compares the K_a values directly, forgetting the square root. 1 assumes equal concentrations give equal acidity. 0.316 inverts the ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', ionisation constants of weak acids

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A saturated solution of a sparingly soluble hydroxide M(OH)₂ in water at 298 K has pH 10.0. The solubility product of M(OH)₂ is (K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴; all the OH⁻ comes from the dissolved hydroxide):

solution.concept: K_sp from the pH of a saturated solution
solution.explanation: pH 10 gives pOH 4, so [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M. Each M(OH)₂ that dissolves gives one M²⁺ and two OH⁻, so [M²⁺] = ½[OH⁻].
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁻¹² takes [M²⁺] equal to [OH⁻]. 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ is just [OH⁻]². 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ forgets to square [OH⁻].
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', solubility equilibria of sparingly soluble salts

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Adding a catalyst to a reaction mixture at equilibrium does not change the composition of the equilibrium mixture.
Reason (R): A catalyst lowers the activation energies of the forward and the backward reactions by the same amount, so it speeds up both reactions equally.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium
solution.explanation: Because both the forward and the backward rates are increased by the same factor, the catalyst only helps the system reach equilibrium sooner; the equilibrium constant and the equilibrium composition stay the same. R explains A.
steps: Catalyst: same lowering of Eₐ for both directions
Both rates rise equally → K unchanged → composition unchanged
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and R gives the reason a catalyst cannot shift an equilibrium.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', effect of a catalyst
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Since HCl is a stronger acid than CH₃COOH, the chloride ion is a stronger base than the acetate ion.
Statement II: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Conjugate acid–base pairs and their strengths
solution.explanation: The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base: Cl⁻ is a much weaker base than CH₃COO⁻, so Statement I is false. NH₃ accepts a proton to give NH₄⁺, its conjugate acid: Statement II is true.
steps: Strong acid ↔ weak conjugate base → Cl⁻ weaker than CH₃COO⁻ → I false
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ → conjugate acid → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I reverses the inverse relation between the strength of an acid and that of its conjugate base.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', Brönsted–Lowry acids and bases
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Water and its vapour are in equilibrium in a closed vessel at a constant temperature, with some liquid left. The volume of the vessel is suddenly increased at the same temperature, liquid water still remaining afterwards. When equilibrium is re-established, the pressure of the water vapour:

options.text: is lower than before, in proportion to the increase in volume
is higher than before, because more liquid evaporates
becomes zero, because the vapour spreads into the extra space

solution.concept: Equilibrium vapour pressure depends only on temperature
solution.explanation: Right after the expansion the vapour pressure falls, so evaporation exceeds condensation; more liquid evaporates until the rates are equal again. That happens at the same equilibrium vapour pressure, which is fixed by the temperature as long as both phases are present.
steps: New equilibrium at the same T → same vapour pressure
solution.why_others_wrong: Boyle's-law reasoning applies only to a fixed amount of gas; here extra liquid evaporates. The vapour pressure does not exceed the equilibrium value or fall to zero while liquid remains.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', equilibrium in physical processes: liquid–vapour equilibrium
solution.final_answer: Option B: is the same as before

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (aqueous solution at 298 K, assuming complete ionisation) with List-II (its pH). (K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)

List-I:
A. 0.01 M HNO₃
B. 0.01 M NaOH
C. 5 × 10⁻⁵ M Ba(OH)₂
D. 5 × 10⁻⁵ M H₂SO₄ (both protons ionised)

List-II:
I. 4
II. 12
III. 2
IV. 10

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: pH of solutions of strong acids and bases
solution.explanation: Find [H₃O⁺] or [OH⁻] from the formula and concentration, then pH = −log[H₃O⁺] and pH = 14 − pOH.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes forget the factor 2 for the dibasic acid or the diacidic base, or mix up pH and pOH.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', the pH scale
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: N₂O₄ partly dissociates on heating: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). At a certain temperature the vapour density of the equilibrium mixture is 38.33 (H = 1). The degree of dissociation of N₂O₄ is (N = 14, O = 16):

solution.concept: Degree of dissociation from the vapour density of an equilibrium mixture
solution.explanation: Starting with 1 mol of N₂O₄, dissociation α gives (1 − α) + 2α = 1 + α mol of gas. The mass is unchanged, so the mean molar mass falls in the ratio 1/(1 + α).
steps: M(N₂O₄) = 92 g mol⁻¹; M(mixture) = 2 × 38.33 = 76.67 g mol⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 16.7% divides the change in molar mass by 92 instead of by 76.67. 40% counts the moles of NO₂ formed (2α). 83.3% is 76.67/92, the reciprocal of 1 + α.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', homogeneous equilibria; equilibrium constant in gaseous systems

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What volume of 0.10 M NaOH must be added to 100 mL of 0.10 M acetic acid at 298 K to obtain a buffer of pH 5.04? (pK_a of CH₃COOH = 4.74; log 2 = 0.30)

solution.concept: Preparing an acidic buffer by part-neutralising a weak acid
solution.explanation: NaOH converts part of the acid into acetate. Henderson equation: pH = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid]); here the ratio must be 10⁰·³⁰ = 2.
steps: Acid taken = 10 mmol; x mmol NaOH gives x mmol CH₃COO⁻ and leaves (10 − x) mmol CH₃COOH
solution.why_others_wrong: 50.0 mL gives a 1 : 1 ratio, i.e. pH = pK_a = 4.74. 33.3 mL gives a salt-to-acid ratio of 1/2 (pH 4.44). 100 mL neutralises all the acid, leaving no buffer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', buffer solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At 298 K, K_sp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. Which of the following arranges the molar solubility of AgCl in the given media in DECREASING order? (The salts NaCl, AgNO₃ and CaCl₂ are completely dissociated.)

options.text: Pure water > 0.020 M CaCl₂ > 0.020 M AgNO₃ > 0.010 M NaCl
Pure water > 0.010 M NaCl > 0.020 M AgNO₃ > 0.020 M CaCl₂
0.020 M CaCl₂ > 0.020 M AgNO₃ > 0.010 M NaCl > Pure water
Pure water > 0.020 M AgNO₃ = 0.020 M CaCl₂ > 0.010 M NaCl

solution.concept: Common ion effect on solubility
solution.explanation: A common ion (Ag⁺ or Cl⁻) lowers the solubility: s ≈ K_sp/[common ion]. The larger the concentration of the common ion, the lower the solubility. 0.020 M CaCl₂ gives 0.040 M Cl⁻.
solution.why_others_wrong: Treating CaCl₂ as giving 0.020 M Cl⁻ (forgetting its two chloride ions) makes it look equal to AgNO₃; the reversed orders put the common-ion media above pure water.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', common ion effect on solubility of ionic salts
solution.final_answer: Option B: Pure water > 0.010 M NaCl > 0.020 M AgNO₃ > 0.020 M CaCl₂

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid.
(b) NH₄⁺ can act as a Brönsted acid.
(c) F⁻ can act as a Lewis base.
(d) BF₃ is a Brönsted acid.
(e) H₃O⁺ is the conjugate base of H₂O.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Lewis and Brönsted–Lowry concepts
solution.explanation: AlCl₃ (aluminium with an incomplete octet) accepts an electron pair: Lewis acid. NH₄⁺ can donate a proton (to give NH₃): Brönsted acid. F⁻ has lone pairs to donate: Lewis base. BF₃ has no hydrogen to donate, so it is a Lewis acid but not a Brönsted acid. H₃O⁺ is the conjugate ACID of H₂O (H₂O + H⁺).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) are wrong; '(a) and (c) only' leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', acids, bases and salts: Brönsted–Lowry and Lewis concepts

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The pH of an aqueous solution of ammonium cyanide, NH₄CN, at 298 K is (pK_a of HCN = 9.31; pK_b of NH₃ = 4.75; pK_w = 14):

solution.concept: pH of a solution of a salt of a weak acid and a weak base
solution.explanation: Both ions hydrolyse; for such a salt pH = 7 + ½(pK_a − pK_b), independent of concentration. CN⁻ (from the much weaker acid HCN) hydrolyses more than NH₄⁺, so the solution is basic.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.72 uses 7 − ½(pK_a − pK_b), the wrong sign. 11.56 leaves out the factor ½. 7.00 assumes the two ions hydrolyse equally, which is true only when pK_a = pK_b.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Equilibrium', hydrolysis of salts and the pH of their solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The average oxidation number of sulphur in the thiosulphate ion, S₂O₃²⁻, is:

solution.concept: Oxidation number from the overall charge
solution.explanation: Take oxygen as −2. The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the atoms equals the charge on the ion.
solution.why_others_wrong: +4 forgets to share the total between the two S atoms. +6 is the value in sulphate. +2.5 is the average in the tetrathionate ion, S₄O₆²⁻.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', oxidation number

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a Daniell cell, the salt bridge that connects the two half-cell solutions usually contains:

options.text: a solution of KCl or NH₄NO₃ set in agar–agar gel

solution.concept: Function and composition of a salt bridge
solution.explanation: The salt bridge is a U-tube filled with a solution of an inert electrolyte such as KCl or NH₄NO₃, usually solidified with agar–agar. Its ions migrate to keep both half-cells electrically neutral and so complete the circuit.
steps: Needs mobile ions that do not react with the half-cell contents → KCl or NH₄NO₃ in agar–agar
solution.why_others_wrong: Pure water hardly conducts; concentrated acid would react and is not used; mercury is a metal conductor, which would not carry ions between the solutions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', galvanic cells
solution.final_answer: Option D: a solution of KCl or NH₄NO₃ set in agar–agar gel

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the reaction 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s), sodium is oxidised.
Reason (R): Each sodium atom loses an electron, and its oxidation number increases from 0 to +1.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Oxidation as loss of electrons / increase in oxidation number
solution.explanation: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, equivalently an increase in oxidation number. Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ is exactly that, so R explains A; chlorine, which gains the electrons, is reduced.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the loss of electrons in R is the definition of the oxidation stated in A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', redox reactions in terms of electron transfer
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: According to Kohlrausch's law, the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the difference between the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and its anion.
Statement II: The conductivity of a solution is the conductance of the volume of solution that contains one mole of the electrolyte.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Kohlrausch's law; conductivity and molar conductivity
solution.explanation: Kohlrausch's law states that Λ°m is the SUM of the individual contributions of the anion and the cation (e.g. Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋): Statement I is false. Conductivity (κ) is the conductance of a unit volume (a 1 cm cube or 1 m cube); the conductance of the volume containing one mole relates to molar conductivity: Statement II is false.
steps: II: describes molar conductivity, not conductivity → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I subtracts where the law adds; Statement II confuses κ with Λm.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', conductance of electrolytic solutions; Kohlrausch's law
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The electrodes of a conductivity cell each have an area of cross-section of 1.2 cm² and are 1.5 cm apart. Filled with a 0.050 mol L⁻¹ solution of an electrolyte, the cell shows a resistance of 500 Ω. The molar conductivity of the solution is:

solution.concept: Cell constant, conductivity and molar conductivity
solution.explanation: Cell constant G* = l/A; κ = G*/R; Λm (S cm² mol⁻¹) = κ (S cm⁻¹) × 1000/c (mol L⁻¹).
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 S cm² mol⁻¹ takes the cell constant as A/l. 0.050 leaves out the factor 1000 (cm³ per litre). 2.5 × 10⁻³ is the conductivity in S cm⁻¹, not the molar conductivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', measurement of the conductivity of ionic solutions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In hot, concentrated alkali, chlorine reacts as 3Cl₂ + 6OH⁻ → 5Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻ + 3H₂O. In this reaction, the ratio of the number of chlorine atoms reduced to the number oxidised is:

solution.concept: Disproportionation: one element is both oxidised and reduced
solution.explanation: Chlorine (oxidation number 0) goes to Cl⁻ (−1, reduction) and to ClO₃⁻ (+5, oxidation). The electrons lost and gained must balance: each Cl oxidised loses 5 electrons, each Cl reduced gains 1.
steps: Cl → Cl⁻: gain of 1 e⁻ each, 5 atoms
Cl → ClO₃⁻ (+5): loss of 5 e⁻, 1 atom
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 5 inverts the ratio. 1 : 1 treats it like Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O, the reaction in cold dilute alkali. 3 : 1 compares Cl₂ molecules with ClO₃⁻.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', types of redox reactions: disproportionation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A zinc rod dipped in copper sulphate solution becomes coated with copper.
Reason (R): The standard reduction potential of Zn²⁺/Zn (−0.76 V) is lower than that of Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Electrochemical series and displacement reactions
solution.explanation: The couple with the lower reduction potential is the stronger reducing agent. Zinc therefore reduces Cu²⁺ ions to copper (which deposits on the rod) and itself goes into solution as Zn²⁺: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V > 0. R explains A.
steps: Cu deposits on the zinc rod
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are true, and the relative electrode potentials are exactly why zinc displaces copper.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Chemistry, 'Redox Reactions', redox reactions and electrode processes; Class 12 Chemistry, 'Electrochemistry', electrochemical series
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
For the Daniell cell Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s) at 298 K, E_cell = E°cell − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]). Match List-I (change) with List-II (effect on E_cell).

List-I:
A. [Cu²⁺] is increased, [Zn²⁺] kept the same
B. [Zn²⁺] is increased, [Cu²⁺] kept the same
